patient_counselling: TIMING IS CRITICAL: start antiviral therapy WITHIN 72 HOURS of rash onset for maximum benefit (reduces severity and duration of acute pain; may reduce postherpetic neuralgia risk). Treatment can still be considered beyond 72h if new vesicles are still forming.
Valacyclovir 1000 mg three times daily for 7 days (preferred — TID is easier than acyclovir's 5×/day, equivalent efficacy, better bioavailability). Take with or without food; stay well hydrated.
Famciclovir 500 mg three times daily for 7 days OR acyclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days — alternatives.

Renal dose adjustment is important: valacyclovir CrCl 30–49 → 1000 mg BID; CrCl 10–29 → 1000 mg OD; CrCl <10 → 500 mg OD. Famciclovir CrCl 40–59 → 500 mg BID; <20 → 250 mg OD. Acyclovir CrCl 25–50 → 800 mg q8h; <10 → 800 mg OD. Confirm renal function.

Pain management: acetaminophen 500–1000 mg q4–6h; NSAIDs (naproxen 250–500 mg BID) if not contraindicated; for severe pain or postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) — refer for gabapentin (start 300 mg TID) or amitriptyline (10–25 mg at bedtime) — these are RX, outside MA scope.
Capsaicin 8% patch is a specialist option for established PHN.
Keep the rash clean and dry; cool compresses can soothe pain; avoid topical antibiotics (interfere with drying); calamine lotion may help itching.

CONTAGIOUSNESS: Shingles is contagious to people who have NEVER had chickenpox or are unvaccinated — the virus in vesicle fluid can cause primary chickenpox (varicella) in them. Avoid contact with: pregnant women without varicella immunity, infants, immunocompromised people, until ALL vesicles are crusted (typically 7–10 days). Cover the rash; practice strict hand hygiene.

SHINGRIX VACCINE (recombinant zoster vaccine, RZV) — recommended after acute episode resolves: NACI 2024 recommends for (a) adults ≥50 years, (b) immunocompromised adults ≥18 years. Two doses 2–6 months apart; 97% effective; preferred even if previous Zostavax was received. Ontario UIIP publicly funded for adults 65–70.

Red flags requiring URGENT referral: rash on the FACE near the eye or tip of nose (Hutchinson's sign — herpes zoster ophthalmicus → same-day ophthalmology to prevent vision loss), ear involvement with facial weakness or hearing loss (Ramsay Hunt syndrome → urgent ENT/neurology), severe disseminated rash (>1 dermatome), signs of CNS involvement (severe headache, confusion, neck stiffness), immunocompromised host.
therapeutic_flow: 1. Confirm Minor Ailments eligibility: Ontario resident with typical unilateral dermatomal vesicular rash within 72h of onset; verify ID/OHIP, obtain consent.

2. Focused history: rash onset and timing (critical — within 72h?), location/dermatome involvement, prodromal pain (often 2–3 days before rash), severity of pain, prior episodes, immune status (HIV, chemo, transplant, prolonged steroids), age, vaccination history (Shingrix, Zostavax), pregnancy/lactation, current medications, renal function.

3. Red flag screen: ophthalmic involvement (Hutchinson's sign — vesicles on tip of nose, eye redness/pain — same-day ophthalmology), Ramsay Hunt syndrome (ear vesicles + facial palsy/hearing loss/vertigo — urgent ENT), disseminated zoster (>1 dermatome — immunocompromise consideration), CNS features (encephalitis), immunocompromised host, pregnancy — refer.

4. Differential diagnosis: rule out herpes simplex (smaller cluster, non-dermatomal), contact dermatitis, impetigo, cellulitis, drug eruption, eczema herpeticum, insect bites; confirm dermatomal pattern.

5. Therapy selection: oral antiviral within 72h — valacyclovir 1000 mg TID × 7 days preferred (renal dose adjusted) OR famciclovir OR acyclovir; pain control with acetaminophen ± NSAIDs; refer for gabapentin/amitriptyline if severe acute pain or PHN; address Shingrix vaccination after recovery.
6. Counsel on antiviral dosing (renal adjustment), 72h timing window, pain control, contagion precautions (until all crusted), Shingrix vaccination plan, red flag recognition (eye, ear, neuro).
7. Document the encounter per OCP standards: assessment findings (dermatome, immunocompetence, days from rash onset), diagnosis, therapy chosen, counselling provided, notify primary care provider.

8. Follow-up: reassess at 7–10 days for resolution; if persistent pain >90 days post-rash → diagnose PHN, refer for management; ensure Shingrix vaccination scheduled after acute episode resolves; reinforce avoidance of contact with susceptible persons until crusted.
